sentences.text: TTCN-3 allows the specification of expressions.
TTCN-3 expressions may be template references, value references or literals (i.e. no operation is involved), and may be composed of the operators defined in clause 7.1.
NOTE: Templates can be used at the RHS of assignment, parameter passing and (predefined) functions where template passing is explicitly allowed.

SingleExpression | 
  "{" { ( FieldReference ":=" ( Expression | "-" )) [","] } "}" | // compound expression
  "{" [ { ( Expression | "-" ) [","] } ] "}" // compound expression
Expressions may be built from other (simple) expressions.
Functions used in expressions shall have a return clause.
The operands of the operators used in an expression shall be values and their root types shall be the types specified for the appropriate operator in the subsequent clauses.
Assignment or list notations are used for expressions of record, set, record of, set of, array, union and anytype types.
In addition to the general static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5, the following restrictions apply:

a) At the point, when an expression is evaluated, the evaluated values of the operands used in expressions shall be completely initialized except where explicitly stated otherwise in the specific clause of the operator.
b) The root types of the operands shall be the types specified for the appropriate operand.
c) With the exception of the equality and non-equality operators, the special value null shall not be used as an operand of expressions (see clause 7.1.3).

This means also that all fields and elements of structured types referenced in an expression shall contain completely initialized values, while other fields and elements, not used in the expression, may be uninitialized or contain omit.

(c_x + c_y – f_increment(c_z))*3  // single expression
  { a:= 1, b:= true }  // compound expression, assignment notation
  { 1, true }  // compound expression, list notation
TTCN-3 supports a number of predefined operators that may be used in the terms of TTCN-3 expressions.
The predefined operators fall into seven categories:
a) arithmetic operators;
b) list operator;
c) relational operators;
d) logical operators;
e) bitwise operators;
f) shift operators;
g) rotate operators;
h) presence checking operators.
In addition to the general static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5, the following restrictions apply:

a) When an expression is evaluated, the evaluated values used as the operands of operators shall be completely initialized, except for those operands for which it is explicitly allowed to be partially initialized (see clause 11.1).

The arithmetic operators represent the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo and remainder.

Operands of these operators shall be of integer values (including derivations of integer) or floating-point numbers (including derivations of float, containing numeric values only), except for mod and rem which shall be used with integer (including derivations of integer) types only.
The usage of the special float values infinity, -infinity and not_a_number in arithmetic operators shall follow the rules defined in IEEE 754 [6].
With integer types, the result type of arithmetic operations is integer.
With float types, the result type of arithmetic operations is float.
In the case where plus (+) or minus (-) is used as the unary operator the rules for operands apply as well.
The result of using the minus operator is the negative value of the operand if it was positive and vice versa.
The result of using the plus operator is the value of the operand, i.e. a positive value if the operand value was positive and a negative value if the operand value was negative.
The result of performing the division operation (/) on two:
a) `integer values gives the whole integer part of the value resulting from dividing the first integer by` the second (i.e. fractions are discarded);
b) numeric float values gives the float value resulting from dividing the first float by the second (i.e. fractions are not discarded).
The operators rem and mod compute on operands of type integer and have a result of type integer.
The operations x rem y and x mod y compute the rest that remains from an integer division of x by y.
Therefore, they are only defined for non-zero operands y.
For positive x and y, both x `rem` `y and x` `mod` `y have the same result but for` negative arguments they differ.
Formally, mod and rem are defined as follows:

x rem y = x - y * (x/y)
  x mod y = x rem |y|  when x >= 0
       = 0  when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0
       = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.
The operation is a simple concatenation from left to right.
No form of arithmetic addition is implied.
The result type is the root type of the operands.
NOTE 1: In case of the list types, both the outer type (i.e. record of, set of or array) and the iterated inner type need to have the same root type in a recursive manner.
NOTE 2: It is also possible to concatenate two or more value list notation expressions if the result is to be used as a record of or array of the same root type as the concatenated expressions.
In addition to the general static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5, the following restrictions apply:
a) When the list concatenation operator is used for record of-s, set of-s and arrays, its operands shall be at least partially initialized.

The predefined relational operators are equality (==), less than (<), greater than (>), non-equality to (!=), greater than or equal to (>=) and less than or equal to (<=).
The result type of all these operations is boolean.

The relational operators less than (<), greater than (>), greater than or equal to (>=), and less than or equal to (<=) shall have only operands of type integer (including derivations of integer), float (including derivations of float), or instances of the same enumerated type.
It is not allowed to compare instances of different root types.

The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.
Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.
The values or field references being compared shall obey the following rules.
This implies that instances of types not mentioned below shall not be operands of equality and non-equality:

Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.
A field reference is equal to a value if the referenced field is initialized with a value and both values are equal.
Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.
Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied.
Enumerated values of the same, or different types can be compared.

In the case of different enumerated types, expression "b" of type "B" can be compared with expression "a" of type "A" if the two types "A" and "B" can be merged to a consistent larger enumerated type (i.e. where numbers are not associated with different identifiers, see also clause 6.3.2.1).
Two enumerated values are equal if and only if both their identifiers and associated integer values (associated either explicitly or implicitly, see clause 6.2.4) are the same.
Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.
The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.
Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied.
The special values -infinity, `infinity and not_a_number are equal to themselves only.
The special` value -infinity is less than any other float value.
The special value infinity is greater than any numerical float values and -infinity.
The special value not_a_number is greater than any other float value (including infinity).
Two charstring or two universal charstring values are equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.

For values of bitstring, hexstring or octetstring types, the same equality rule applies as for charstring values with the exception, that fractions which shall equal at all positions are bits, hexadecimal digits or pairs of hexadecimal digits accordingly.

Two record values, or set values are equal respectively if and only if they are mutually compatible with the type of the other operand (see clause 6.3.2.2), the actual values of all present fields are equal to their corresponding fields and all fields corresponding to omitted fields are also omitted in the peer value.

Two record of values, set of values or array values, respectively, are equal if and only if they are mutually compatible with the type of the other operand (see clause 6.3.2.3), they both have the same length, and each element of one value is equal to the corresponding element of the other value.
Record of values and array values may also be compared, in which case the corresponding record of type of the array is being considered.

Values of the same union type, and values of different union types in which at least one of the alternatives is compatible with the other type (see clause 6.3.2.4) can be compared (independent if a compatible alternative is the selected one or not).

Two values of union types are equal if and only if in both values the name of the selected alternative is identical, they are compatible with the type of the other value, and the actual values of the chosen fields are equal.
Values of the same or any two anytype types can be compared.

For anytype values the same rule apply as to union values, with the addition that names of user-defined types defined with the same name in different modules do not denote the same type name of the selected alternatives.

Two default, two port, two timer or two component values are equal if and only if they both are initialized with the special value null or they both contain a reference to the same entity (i.e. they designate the same default, port, timer or test component, independent of the actual state of the denoted object).
It is also possible to use compound expressions (field assignment or value list notation) directly as operands of comparison operations of structured types.

If there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator, they shall both be value list notation expressions where the elements shall be of the same root type and they shall be compared like record of values with elements of that root type.
If only one operand of the comparison operation is a compound expression it shall be compatible with the root type of the other operand and they shall be compared like values of that root type.

Two maps are equal if and only if they are mutually compatible with the type of the other operand (see clause 6.3.2.2), they have the same number of key-value pairs and for each key-value pair in both maps there is a key-value pair in the other map where the key from one pair is equal to the key from the other pair and the value from one pair is equal to the value from the other pair.

The predefined boolean operators perform the operations of negation, logical and, logical or and logical xor.
Their operands shall be of root type boolean.
The result type of logical operations is boolean.
The logical not is the unary operator that returns the value true if its operand was of value false and returns the value false if the operand was of value true.
The logical and returns the value true if both its operands are true; otherwise it returns the value false.
The logical or returns the value true if at least one of its operands is true; it returns the value false only if both operands are false.
The logical xor returns the value true if one of its operands is true; it returns the value false if both operands are false or if both operands are true.

Short circuit evaluation for boolean expressions is used, i.e. the evaluation of operands of logical operators is stopped once the overall result is known: in the case of the and operator, if the left argument evaluates to false, then the right argument is not evaluated and the whole expression evaluates to false.
In the case of the or operator, if the left argument evaluates to true, then the right argument is not evaluated and the whole expression evaluates to true.
The predefined bitwise operators perform the operations of bitwise not, bitwise and, bitwise or and bitwise xor.
These operators are known as not4b, and4b, or4b and xor4b respectively.
NOTE: To be read as "not for bit", "and for bit", etc.
Their operands shall be of root type `bitstring, hexstring or octetstring.
In the case of and4b, or4b and` xor4b the operands shall be of the same root types.The result type of the bitwise operators shall be the root type of the operands.
The bitwise not4b unary operator inverts the individual bit values of its operand.
For each bit in the operand a 1 bit is set to 0 and a 0 bit is set to 1.
That is:

not4b '1'B gives '0'B
  not4b '0'B gives '1'B
EXAMPLE 1:

not4b '1010'B gives '0101'B
  not4b '1A5'H gives 'E5A'H
  not4b '01A5'O gives 'FE5A'O
The bitwise and4b operator accepts two operands of equal length.
For each corresponding bit position, the resulting value is a 1 if both bits are set to 1, otherwise the value for the resulting bit is 0.
That is:

'1'B and4b '1'B gives '1'B
  '1'B and4b '0'B gives '0'B
  '0'B and4b '1'B gives '0'B
  '0'B and4b '0'B gives '0'B
EXAMPLE 2:

'1001'B and4b '0101'B gives '0001'B
  'B'H and4b '5'H gives '1'H
  'FB'O and4b '15'O gives '11'O
The bitwise or4b operator accepts two operands of equal length.
For each corresponding bit position, the resulting value is 0 if both bits are set to 0, otherwise the value for the resulting bit is 1.
That is:

'1'B or4b '1'B gives '1'B
  '1'B or4b '0'B gives '1'B
  '0'B or4b '1'B gives '1'B
  '0'B or4b '0'B gives '0'B
EXAMPLE 3:

'1001'B or4b '0101'B gives '1101'B
  '9'H or4b '5'H gives 'D'H
  'A9'O or4b 'F5'O gives 'FD'O
The bitwise xor4b operator accepts two operands of equal length.
For each corresponding bit position, the resulting value is 0 if both bits are set to 0 or if both bits are set to 1, otherwise the value for the resulting bit is 1.
That is:

'1'B xor4b '1'B gives '0'B
  '0'B xor4b '0'B gives '0'B
  '0'B xor4b '1'B gives '1'B
  '1'B xor4b '0'B gives '1'B
EXAMPLE 4:

'1001'B xor4b '0101'B gives '1100'B
  '9'H xor4b '5'H gives 'C'H
  '39'O xor4b '15'O gives '2C'O
The predefined shift operators perform the shift left (<<) and shift right (>>)operations.
Their left-hand operand shall be of root type `bitstring, hexstring or octetstring.
Their right-hand operand shall be a non-negative` integer.
The result type of these operators shall be the same as the root type of the left operand.
The shift operators behave differently based upon the type of their left-hand operand.
If the type of the left-hand operand is:
a) `bitstring then the shift unit applied is 1 bit;` b) `hexstring then the shift unit applied is 1 hexadecimal digit;` c) `octetstring then the shift unit applied is 1 octet.`
The shift left (<<) operator accepts two operands.
It shifts the left-hand operand by the number of shift units to the left as specified by the right-hand operand.
Excess shift units (bits, hexadecimal digits or octets) are discarded.
For each shift unit shifted to the left, a zero ('0'B, '0'H, or '00'O determined according to the type of the left-hand operand) is inserted from the right-hand side of the left operand.
EXAMPLE 1:
The shift right (>>)operator accepts two operands.
It shifts the left-hand operand by the number of shift units to the right as specified by the right-hand operand.
Excess shift units (bits, hexadecimal digits or octets) are discarded.
For each shift unit shifted to the right, a zero ('0'B, '0'H, or '00'O determined according to the type of the left-hand operand) is inserted from the left-hand side of the left operand.
EXAMPLE 2:
The predefined rotate operators perform the rotate left (<@) and rotate right (@>) operators.
Their left-hand operand shall be of root type bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring, universal `charstring,` record of, or set of.
Their right-hand operand shall be a non-negative integer.
The result type of these operators shall be the same as the root type of the left-hand operand.
NOTE 1: Note that the root types of arrays is record of, therefore arrays are allowed as left-hand operands of rotate operators.
The rotate operators behave differently based upon the type of their left-hand operand.
If the type of the left-hand operand is:

a) `bitstring then the rotate unit applied is 1 bit;` b) `hexstring then the rotate unit applied is 1 hexadecimal digit;` c) `octetstring then the rotate unit applied is 1 octet;` d) `charstring or universal` `charstring then the rotate unit applied is one character;` e) `record of, set of, or array then the rotate unit applied is one element.`
The rotate left (<@) operator accepts two operands.
It rotates the left-hand operand by the number of shift units to the left as specified by the right-hand operand.
Excess shift units (bits, hexadecimal digits, octets, characters, or elements) are re-inserted into the left-hand operand from its right-hand side.
In addition to the general static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5, the following restrictions apply:
a) When the rotate operator is used for record of-s, set of-s and arrays, its left hand operand shall be at least partially initialized.
NOTE 2: Note that for the right hand operand restriction a) in clause 6.5 further on applies.
EXAMPLE 1:
The rotate right (@>) operator accepts two operands.
It rotates the left-hand operand by the number of shift units to the right as specified by the right-hand operand.
Excess shift units (bits, hexadecimal digits, octets, characters, or elements) are re-inserted into the left-hand operand from its left-hand side.

The presence checking operators include ispresent, ischosen, isvalue and isbound operators.
The result type of the presence checking operators is boolean.
The operand of these operators can be of any type.

Specific rules apply if the operand of a presence checking operator is a data object reference, function instance, template instance or a result of the valueof operation followed by an ExtendedFieldReference.

In these cases, if resolving dot notation, index notation (see clause 7.2) or decoded field references (see clause 7.3) included in the _ExtendedFieldReference would produce an error (e.g. if an index is out of range, when referencing a sub-field of an_ omitted field etc.), the following happens:
No error is produced.
Evaluation of all remaining unresolved fields in the ExtendedFieldReference is stopped.
All remaining parts of the ExtendedFieldReference that are located right from the operation that would normally produce an error up to the end of the presence checking operator are not evaluated.
The presence checking operator yields the value false.
The rule on special handling of dot notation, index notation and decoded field references is not applied recursively.
Errors occurring during resolving a value of an index inside index notation or a value of an encoding format parameter of a decoded field reference are not affected by this rule.
The ispresent operator checks whether a referenced field is present in a data object.
ispresent "(" TemplateInstance ")"
The ispresent operator returns:
the value true if the operand fulfils the (present) template restriction as described in clause 15.8;
the value false otherwise.
NOTE 1: When the argument of ispresent is a subfield of a template field to which the "?" (AnyValue) matching is assigned, the extension mechanism specified in clause 15.6.2 applies.
NOTE 2: This means that whenever ispresent(m_myTemplate) returns true:

m_myTemplate can safely be assigned to a non-optional field of the type of the template in a template variable; m_myTemplate can safely be used as an actual template(present) parameter or assigned to a variable of kind template(present).
General static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5 apply.
EXAMPLE:
The ischosen operator checks whether a referenced alternative is present in a data object.
ischosen "(" TemplateInstance ")"
This operator is allowed for data objects of all data types that are a union-field-reference or a type alternative of an anytype.
The operator returns:
the value true if and only if the data object reference specifies the variant of the union type or the type alternative of the anytype that is actually selected for the given data object;
in all other cases false.
The ischosen operator is applicable to data objects of union types or of anytype containing a specific value or a value list.
In case of a value list, the operator returns true if all data objects present in the value list have the given alternative selected.
The result is false if there is another alternative of the union type or anytype on which ischosen would return true.

NOTE: Note that in case of anytype-s, no type compatibility is considered when determining the selected alternative; i.e. at the evaluation only the exact type chosen for the given value will satisfy the above criteria.
General static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5 apply.

The isvalue operator checks whether a referenced data object is a specific value.
isvalue "(" TemplateInstance ")"
The isvalue operator yields true, if the operand is completely initialized and resolves to a specific value.
If the operand is of record or set type, omitted optional fields shall be considered as initialized, i.e. the operator shall also yield true if optional fields of the operand are set to omit.
The operator shall yield false otherwise.
The specific value null is considered as concrete value.
General static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5 apply.
EXAMPLE 1: Simple types:

template charstring m_char0 := "ABCD"; //template containing a specific value matching
  template charstring m_char1 := "AB?D"; //template containing a specific value matching
                          //note, that "?" is not a matching symbol in this case
  template charstring mw_char2 := pattern "ABCD"; // a pattern matching a single value only
  template charstring mw_char3 := pattern "AB?D"; // pattern matching
  template charstring m_char4 := ("ABCD"); // template containing a specific value (expression)
  template charstring mw_char5 := ("ABCD","EFGH"); // a value list matching a single value only
  var boolean v_checkResult := isvalue(m_char0); // yields true
  v_checkResult := isvalue(m_char1); // yields true
  v_checkResult := isvalue(mw_char2); // yields false
  v_checkResult := isvalue(mw_char3); // yields false
  v_checkResult := isvalue(m_char4); // yields true
  v_checkResult := isvalue(mw_char5); // yields false
EXAMPLE 2: Special types:

var default v_default := null;
  var boolean v_checkResult := isvalue(v_default); // yields true

The isbound operator checks whether a referenced data object is at least partially initialized.
isbound "(" TemplateInstance ")"
The isbound operator yields true, if the operand is at least partially initialized.
If the operand is of a record or
set type, omitted optional fields shall be considered as initialized, i.e. the operator shall also yield true if at least one
optional field of the operand is set to omit.
The operator shall yield false otherwise.

Inaccessible fields (e.g. non-selected alternatives of union types, subfields of omitted record and set types or subfields of non-selected union fields) shall be considered as uninitialized, i.e. isbound shall yield for them false.
The specific value null is considered as concrete value.
EXAMPLE 1: Simple types

var template charstring v_char; 
  var boolean_checkResult := isbound(v_char); // yields false as v_char is uninitialized
  v_char := "AB?D";              // template containing a specific value
  checkResult := isbound(v_char);       // yields true
  v_char := pattern "AB?D";          // template containing a pattern matching
  checkResult := isbound(v_char);       // yields true
EXAMPLE 2: Special types

var default v_default := null;
  var boolean_checkResult := isbound(v_default); // yields true
EXAMPLE 3: Record/set types
Within expressions, fields of record and set types are referenced with the dot notation ".field".
Elements of record of, set of, array and string types are referenced with the index notation "[index]".
Dot and brackets have the same binding power.
Field references and list elements are evaluated from left to right.
Decoded field reference is a specific notation called decoding notation that can be applied to expressions of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring or universal charstring types.
It is used for accessing content of implicitly decoded payload fields.

ReferencedValue "=>" ( PredefinedType | TypeIdentifier | 
     ( "(" Type [ "," Expression ] ")" ) )
The ReferencedValue preceding the => symbol in a decoding notation shall be decoded into a value of the type following the => symbol.
Failure of this decoding shall cause a test case error.
In case the ReferencedValue is of the
universal charstring type and the extended syntax with parentheses is used, the Type can be followed by an
optional parameter defining the encoding format.
The parameter shall be of the charstring type and it shall contain one of the strings allowed for the decvalue_unichar function (specified in clause C.5.4).
Any other value shall cause an error.
In case the ReferencedValue is not a universal `charstring, the optional parameter shall not be` present.
In addition to the general static rules of TTCN-3 given in clause 5, the following restrictions apply:
a) If the type following the => symbol is not enclosed into parentheses, only a built-in type or a type reference consisting of a single identifier can be used.
Extended type references shall always use the extended syntax with parentheses.

entities.name: record of, set of or array value

requirements.subject: ent:function

requirements.subject: ent:operand
requirements.canonical: An operand of an operator used in an expression SHALL be a value.
requirements.original: The operands of the operators used in an expression shall be values and their root types shall be the types specified for the appropriate operator in the subsequent clauses.

ambiguity.issue: The general rule conflicts with operators such as `isvalue`, `ispresent`, `ischosen` and `isbound`, which accept template instances as operands; reading 1 (rule applies except where an operator clause states otherwise) is chosen.

requirements.subject: ent:operand
requirements.canonical: The root type of an operand of an operator used in an expression SHALL be one of the types specified for that operator in clauses 7.1.1 to 7.1.8.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression

requirements.original: Assignment or list notations are used for expressions of record, set, record of, set of, array, union and anytype types.

ambiguity.issue: It is unclear whether both notations apply to every listed type; list notation is not allowed for union and anytype, and assignment notation is not used for record of/set of/array (which use index notation). Reading 1 is chosen.

requirements.original: b) The root types of the operands shall be the types specified for the appropriate operand.

ambiguity.issue: The sentence says 'types specified for the appropriate operand', where 'appropriate operator' is meant (compare 7.0-s007); it restates 7.0-007b.

requirements.subject: ent:mod-operator
requirements.canonical: The result type of the `rem` and `mod` operators IS integer.
requirements.original: The operators rem and mod compute on operands of type integer and have a result of type integer.

requirements.subject: ent:rem-operator
requirements.canonical: The result of `x rem y` and of `x mod y` IS the remainder of the integer division of x by y.
requirements.original: The operations x rem y and x mod y compute the rest that remains from an integer division of x by y.

requirements.subject: ent:rem-operator
requirements.canonical: The right operand y of the `rem` or `mod` operator SHALL NOT be zero.
requirements.original: Therefore, they are only defined for non-zero operands y.

ambiguity.issue: 'only defined for non-zero operands y' does not say whether a zero divisor is a compile-time error (for constants) or a runtime error, or whether the result is just undefined.
readings: A zero right operand of `rem` or `mod` SHALL cause an error (at compile time if known statically, otherwise at runtime).
The result of `rem` or `mod` with a zero right operand IS undefined and no error is required.

requirements.subject: ent:rem-operator
requirements.canonical: For positive x and y, `x rem y` IS equal to `x mod y`; for negative arguments the results differ.
requirements.original: For positive x and y, both x `rem` `y and x` `mod` `y have the same result but for` negative arguments they differ.

requirements.subject: ent:rem-operator
requirements.canonical: `x rem y` IS defined as `x - y * (x/y)`.
requirements.original:
x rem y = x - y * (x/y)
  x mod y = x rem |y|  when x >= 0
       = 0  when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0
       = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.subject: ent:mod-operator
requirements.canonical: When x >= 0, `x mod y` IS equal to `x rem |y|`.
requirements.original:
x rem y = x - y * (x/y)
  x mod y = x rem |y|  when x >= 0
       = 0  when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0
       = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.subject: ent:mod-operator
requirements.condition: x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0
requirements.canonical: When x < 0 and `x rem |y|` = 0, `x mod y` IS 0.
requirements.original:
x rem y = x - y * (x/y)
  x mod y = x rem |y|  when x >= 0
       = 0  when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0
       = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.subject: ent:mod-operator
requirements.condition: x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0
requirements.canonical: When x < 0 and `x rem |y|` < 0, `x mod y` IS `|y| + x rem |y|`.
requirements.original:
x rem y = x - y * (x/y)
  x mod y = x rem |y|  when x >= 0
       = 0  when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0
       = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.subject: ent:mod-operator
requirements.canonical: For x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 the value of `x mod 3` IS 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0 respectively.

requirements.subject: ent:rem-operator
requirements.canonical: For x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 the value of `x rem 3` IS 0, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 0 respectively.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.canonical: The list operator `&` IS the concatenation of values of string types, record of types, set of types or arrays.
requirements.original: The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.

ambiguity.issue: 'array of' is used for arrays; 'string types' is not a glossary term (bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring, universal charstring are meant).

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.canonical: The operands of the list operator `&` SHALL be of the same root type.
requirements.original: The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.canonical: The list operator `&` IS a simple concatenation of its operands from left to right.
requirements.original: The operation is a simple concatenation from left to right.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.canonical: The list operator `&` IS NOT any form of arithmetic addition.
requirements.original: No form of arithmetic addition is implied.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.canonical: The result type of the list operator `&` IS the root type of its operands.
requirements.original: The result type is the root type of the operands.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.condition: the operands are of a record of, set of or array type
requirements.canonical: When the list operator `&` is applied to record of, set of or array values, both the outer type and the iterated inner type of the operands SHALL have the same root type, recursively.
requirements.original: NOTE 1: In case of the list types, both the outer type (i.e. record of, set of or array) and the iterated inner type need to have the same root type in a recursive manner.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.canonical: Two or more value list notation expressions CAN be concatenated with `&` if the result is used as a record of or array of the same root type as the concatenated expressions.
requirements.original: NOTE 2: It is also possible to concatenate two or more value list notation expressions if the result is to be used as a record of or array of the same root type as the concatenated expressions.

requirements.subject: ent:list-operator
requirements.condition: the operands are record of, set of or array values
requirements.canonical: When the list operator `&` is used for record of, set of or array values, its operands SHALL be at least partially initialized.
requirements.original: a) When the list concatenation operator is used for record of-s, set of-s and arrays, its operands shall be at least partially initialized.

requirements.subject: ent:relational-operator
requirements.canonical: The relational operators ARE equality (==), less than (<), greater than (>), non-equality (!=), greater than or equal to (>=) and less than or equal to (<=).
requirements.original: The predefined relational operators are equality (==), less than (<), greater than (>), non-equality to (!=), greater than or equal to (>=) and less than or equal to (<=).

requirements.subject: ent:relational-operator
requirements.canonical: The result type of a relational operator IS boolean.
requirements.original: The result type of all these operations is boolean.

requirements.subject: ent:ordering-operator
requirements.condition: the operator is <, >, >= or <=
requirements.canonical: An operand of the relational operators <, >, >= and <= SHALL be of type integer (including types derived from integer), of type float (including types derived from float), or an instance of the same enumerated type as the other operand.
requirements.original: The relational operators less than (<), greater than (>), greater than or equal to (>=), and less than or equal to (<=) shall have only operands of type integer (including derivations of integer), float (including derivations of float), or instances of the same enumerated type.

requirements.subject: ent:relational-operator
requirements.canonical: The operands of a relational operator SHALL NOT be instances of different root types.
requirements.original: It is not allowed to compare instances of different root types.

ambiguity.issue: The sentence follows the rule for <, >, >=, <= but does not say whether it also covers == and !=; for == and != the next paragraph makes an exception for enumerated types. Chosen reading: it applies to <, >, >= and <=.
readings: The operands of the relational operators <, >, >= and <= SHALL NOT be instances of different root types.
The operands of any relational operator, including == and !=, SHALL NOT be instances of different root types.

requirements.subject: ent:address-type
requirements.canonical: A value of the address type MAY be an operand of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of the actual type of the address type.
requirements.original: The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.

requirements.subject: ent:address-type
requirements.condition: the actual type of the address type differs from the types specified above
requirements.canonical: If the actual type of the address type differs from the types for which equality is defined, a value of the address type SHALL only be compared with the special value `null`.
requirements.original: The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.

ambiguity.issue: "the types specified above" can mean the operand types of <, >, >=, <= (integer, float, enumerated) given in the previous paragraph, or the types for which equality rules are given in the list below. Chosen reading: the types for which equality rules exist.
readings: If the actual type of the address type is not one of the types for which equality is defined in clause 7.1.3, an address value SHALL only be compared with `null`.
If the actual type of the address type is not integer, float or an enumerated type, an address value SHALL only be compared with `null`.

requirements.subject: ent:equality-operator
requirements.canonical: An operand of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators SHALL be a completely initialized value or a field reference.
requirements.original: Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.

requirements.subject: ent:equality-operator
requirements.condition: the operands are not of enumerated types
requirements.canonical: Except for enumerated types, the operands of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators SHALL be of compatible root types.
requirements.original: Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.

ambiguity.issue: "compatible root types" is not a defined term; clause 6.3 defines type compatibility between types, not between root types.

requirements.subject: ent:equality-operator
requirements.canonical: An instance of a type for which no equality rule is given in clause 7.1.3 SHALL NOT be an operand of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators.
requirements.original: This implies that instances of types not mentioned below shall not be operands of equality and non-equality: The values or field references being compared shall obey the following rules.

ambiguity.issue: The list of equality rules does not mention boolean, verdicttype, objid or address types. Taken literally, these types could not be compared with == and !=, which is surely not intended. Chosen reading: the literal one, but with an open issue for the types that are not listed.
readings: Only instances of the types listed in the equality rules of clause 7.1.3 MAY be operands of == and !=; values of boolean, verdicttype or objid types SHALL NOT be compared.
Values of basic types not listed (e.g. boolean, verdicttype) MAY be compared with == and != with obvious value equality; only types without a defined equality SHALL NOT be operands.

requirements.subject: ent:field-reference
requirements.canonical: Two field references ARE equal if both referenced fields are optional fields and both are set to `omit`.
requirements.original: Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.

requirements.subject: ent:field-reference
requirements.canonical: Two field references ARE equal if both referenced fields, optional or not, are initialized with values and these values are equal.
requirements.original: Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.

requirements.subject: ent:field-reference
requirements.canonical: A field reference IS equal to a value if the referenced field is initialized with a value and both values are equal.
requirements.original: A field reference is equal to a value if the referenced field is initialized with a value and both values are equal.

requirements.subject: ent:integer-value
requirements.canonical: Two integer values ARE equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.original: Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.subject: ent:integer-value
requirements.canonical: Integer values ARE ordered by the normal mathematical ordering for the relational operators <, >, >= and <=.
requirements.original: Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied. Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.subject: ent:enumerated-value
requirements.canonical: Enumerated values of the same enumerated type or of different enumerated types MAY be compared.
requirements.original: Enumerated values of the same, or different types can be compared.

requirements.subject: ent:enumerated-value
requirements.condition: the operands are of different enumerated types
requirements.canonical: An expression of enumerated type B SHALL only be compared with an expression of a different enumerated type A if A and B can be merged into a consistent larger enumerated type, i.e. no integer value is associated with different identifiers.
requirements.original: In the case of different enumerated types, expression "b" of type "B" can be compared with expression "a" of type "A" if the two types "A" and "B" can be merged to a consistent larger enumerated type (i.e. where numbers are not associated with different identifiers, see also clause 6.3.2.1).

ambiguity.issue: In EXAMPLE 1, EDesWeekDays and EWeekDays associate the same numbers with different identifiers and therefore cannot be merged, yet the comparison v_myDesWeekDayMon == v_myWeekDayMon is shown as returning false and not as an error. Chosen reading: the normative text (comparison is not allowed).
readings: Comparing values of two enumerated types that cannot be merged SHALL cause an error.
Values of two enumerated types that cannot be merged MAY be compared, and the comparison returns false.

requirements.subject: ent:enumerated-value
requirements.canonical: Two enumerated values ARE equal if and only if both their identifiers and their associated integer values, associated explicitly or implicitly, are the same.
requirements.original: Two enumerated values are equal if and only if both their identifiers and associated integer values (associated either explicitly or implicitly, see clause 6.2.4) are the same.

requirements.subject: ent:float-value
requirements.canonical: Two float values ARE equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.original: Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.subject: ent:minus-zero
requirements.canonical: The float values minus zero and plus zero ARE two distinct values.
requirements.original: The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.

requirements.subject: ent:minus-zero
requirements.canonical: The float value minus zero IS less than plus zero, which represents zero.
requirements.original: The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.

requirements.subject: ent:float-value
requirements.canonical: Float values other than the special values ARE ordered by the normal mathematical ordering.
requirements.original: Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied. Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.subject: ent:special-float-value
requirements.canonical: Each of the special float values -infinity, infinity and not_a_number IS equal only to itself.
requirements.original: The special values -infinity, `infinity and not_a_number are equal to themselves only.

requirements.subject: ent:minus-infinity
requirements.canonical: The special value -infinity IS less than any other float value.
requirements.original: The special` value -infinity is less than any other float value.

requirements.subject: ent:infinity
requirements.canonical: The special value infinity IS greater than any numerical float value and greater than -infinity.
requirements.original: The special value infinity is greater than any numerical float values and -infinity.

requirements.subject: ent:not-a-number
requirements.canonical: The special value not_a_number IS greater than any other float value, including infinity.
requirements.original: The special value not_a_number is greater than any other float value (including infinity).

requirements.subject: ent:charstring-value
requirements.canonical: Two charstring values, or two universal charstring values, ARE equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.
requirements.original: Two charstring or two universal charstring values are equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.

requirements.subject: ent:string-value
requirements.canonical: Two bitstring, two hexstring or two octetstring values ARE equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the bits, hexadecimal digits or octets, respectively, at all positions are the same.
requirements.original: For values of bitstring, hexstring or octetstring types, the same equality rule applies as for charstring values with the exception, that fractions which shall equal at all positions are bits, hexadecimal digits or pairs of hexadecimal digits accordingly. Two charstring or two universal charstring values are equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.

ambiguity.issue: "fractions" is used for the string elements, and "pairs of hexadecimal digits" for octets.

requirements.subject: ent:record-value
requirements.canonical: Two record values, or two set values, ARE equal if and only if each is compatible with the type of the other operand, the actual values of all present fields are equal to their corresponding fields, and all fields corresponding to omitted fields are also omitted in the other value.
requirements.original: Two record values, or set values are equal respectively if and only if they are mutually compatible with the type of the other operand (see clause 6.3.2.2), the actual values of all present fields are equal to their corresponding fields and all fields corresponding to omitted fields are also omitted in the peer value.

requirements.subject: ent:record-of-value
requirements.canonical: Two record of values, two set of values or two array values ARE equal if and only if each is compatible with the type of the other operand, both have the same length, and each element of one value is equal to the corresponding element of the other value.
requirements.original: Two record of values, set of values or array values, respectively, are equal if and only if they are mutually compatible with the type of the other operand (see clause 6.3.2.3), they both have the same length, and each element of one value is equal to the corresponding element of the other value.

requirements.subject: ent:record-of-value
requirements.canonical: A record of value and an array value MAY be compared; in this case the array is treated as a value of its corresponding record of type.
requirements.original: Record of values and array values may also be compared, in which case the corresponding record of type of the array is being considered.

requirements.subject: ent:union-value
requirements.canonical: Values of the same union type, and values of different union types in which at least one alternative is compatible with the other type, MAY be compared, independent of whether a compatible alternative is the selected one.
requirements.original: Values of the same union type, and values of different union types in which at least one of the alternatives is compatible with the other type (see clause 6.3.2.4) can be compared (independent if a compatible alternative is the selected one or not).

ambiguity.issue: "at least one of the alternatives is compatible with the other type" does not say whether an alternative of one union must be compatible with an alternative (with the same name) of the other union, or with the other union type as a whole. Chosen reading: per clause 6.3.2.4, an alternative with the same name and a compatible type.
readings: Values of different union types MAY be compared if at least one alternative of one union type has the same name and a compatible type as an alternative of the other union type.
Values of different union types MAY be compared if the type of at least one alternative of one union type is compatible with the other union type.

requirements.subject: ent:union-value
requirements.canonical: Values of different union types in which no alternative is compatible with the other type SHALL NOT be compared.
requirements.original: Values of the same union type, and values of different union types in which at least one of the alternatives is compatible with the other type (see clause 6.3.2.4) can be compared (independent if a compatible alternative is the selected one or not).

requirements.subject: ent:union-value
requirements.canonical: Two union values ARE equal if and only if the names of the selected alternatives are identical, each value is compatible with the type of the other value, and the actual values of the selected alternatives are equal.
requirements.original: Two values of union types are equal if and only if in both values the name of the selected alternative is identical, they are compatible with the type of the other value, and the actual values of the chosen fields are equal.

requirements.subject: ent:anytype-value
requirements.canonical: Values of the same anytype, or of the anytypes of any two modules, MAY be compared.
requirements.original: Values of the same or any two anytype types can be compared.

ambiguity.issue: "any two anytype types" refers to the anytype of different modules; anytype is a single type per module.

requirements.subject: ent:anytype-value
requirements.canonical: Two anytype values ARE equal according to the same rules as union values.
requirements.original: For anytype values the same rule apply as to union values, with the addition that names of user-defined types defined with the same name in different modules do not denote the same type name of the selected alternatives.

requirements.subject: ent:anytype-value
requirements.canonical: In the comparison of anytype values, user-defined types with the same name defined in different modules DO NOT denote the same selected alternative name.
requirements.original: For anytype values the same rule apply as to union values, with the addition that names of user-defined types defined with the same name in different modules do not denote the same type name of the selected alternatives.

requirements.subject: ent:reference-value
requirements.canonical: Two default, two port, two timer or two component values ARE equal if and only if both are initialized with the special value `null` or both refer to the same default, port, timer or test component, independent of the actual state of that object.
requirements.original: Two default, two port, two timer or two component values are equal if and only if they both are initialized with the special value null or they both contain a reference to the same entity (i.e. they designate the same default, port, timer or test component, independent of the actual state of the denoted object).

ambiguity.issue: "default, port, timer or component values" are references to objects; the glossary term is object reference.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression
requirements.canonical: A compound expression (assignment notation or value list notation) MAY be used directly as an operand of a comparison operation of a structured type.
requirements.original: It is also possible to use compound expressions (field assignment or value list notation) directly as operands of comparison operations of structured types.

ambiguity.issue: "field assignment" is used for the glossary term assignment notation.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression
requirements.condition: there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator
requirements.canonical: If both operands of a comparison operator are compound expressions, both SHALL be value list notation expressions.
requirements.original: If there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator, they shall both be value list notation expressions where the elements shall be of the same root type and they shall be compared like record of values with elements of that root type.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression
requirements.condition: there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator
requirements.canonical: If both operands of a comparison operator are value list notation expressions, all their elements SHALL be of the same root type.
requirements.original: If there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator, they shall both be value list notation expressions where the elements shall be of the same root type and they shall be compared like record of values with elements of that root type.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression
requirements.condition: there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator
requirements.canonical: If both operands of a comparison operator are value list notation expressions, they ARE compared like record of values whose element type is the common root type of the elements.
requirements.original: If there is a compound expression on both sides of the comparison operator, they shall both be value list notation expressions where the elements shall be of the same root type and they shall be compared like record of values with elements of that root type.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression
requirements.condition: only one operand is a compound expression
requirements.canonical: If only one operand of a comparison operation is a compound expression, the compound expression SHALL be compatible with the root type of the other operand.
requirements.original: If only one operand of the comparison operation is a compound expression it shall be compatible with the root type of the other operand and they shall be compared like values of that root type.

requirements.subject: ent:compound-expression
requirements.condition: only one operand is a compound expression
requirements.canonical: If only one operand of a comparison operation is a compound expression, the operands ARE compared like values of the root type of the other operand.
requirements.original: If only one operand of the comparison operation is a compound expression it shall be compatible with the root type of the other operand and they shall be compared like values of that root type.

requirements.subject: ent:map-value
requirements.canonical: Two map values ARE equal if and only if each is compatible with the type of the other operand, they have the same number of key-value pairs, and for each key-value pair in either map the other map has a key-value pair with an equal key and an equal value.
requirements.original: Two maps are equal if and only if they are mutually compatible with the type of the other operand (see clause 6.3.2.2), they have the same number of key-value pairs and for each key-value pair in both maps there is a key-value pair in the other map where the key from one pair is equal to the key from the other pair and the value from one pair is equal to the value from the other pair.

ambiguity.issue: The cross-reference to clause 6.3.2.2 (compatibility of record and set types) is used for map types.

requirements.subject: ent:boolean-operator
requirements.canonical: The boolean operators ARE negation (`not`), logical and (`and`), logical or (`or`) and logical xor (`xor`).
requirements.original: The predefined boolean operators perform the operations of negation, logical and, logical or and logical xor.

requirements.subject: ent:boolean-operator
requirements.canonical: An operand of a boolean operator SHALL be of root type boolean.
requirements.original: Their operands shall be of root type boolean.

requirements.subject: ent:boolean-operator
requirements.canonical: The result type of a boolean operator IS boolean.
requirements.original: The result type of logical operations is boolean.

requirements.subject: ent:not-operator
requirements.canonical: The unary `not` operator returns `true` if its operand is `false` and returns `false` if its operand is `true`.
requirements.original: The logical not is the unary operator that returns the value true if its operand was of value false and returns the value false if the operand was of value true.

requirements.subject: ent:and-operator
requirements.canonical: The `and` operator returns `true` if both operands are `true`, and `false` otherwise.
requirements.original: The logical and returns the value true if both its operands are true; otherwise it returns the value false.

requirements.subject: ent:or-operator
requirements.canonical: The `or` operator returns `true` if at least one operand is `true`, and `false` only if both operands are `false`.
requirements.original: The logical or returns the value true if at least one of its operands is true; it returns the value false only if both operands are false.

requirements.subject: ent:xor-operator
requirements.canonical: The `xor` operator returns `true` if exactly one operand is `true`, and `false` if both operands are `false` or both are `true`.
requirements.original: The logical xor returns the value true if one of its operands is true; it returns the value false if both operands are false or if both operands are true.

requirements.subject: ent:short-circuit-evaluation
requirements.canonical: The evaluation of the operands of a boolean operator IS stopped once the overall result is known (short circuit evaluation).
requirements.original: Short circuit evaluation for boolean expressions is used, i.e. the evaluation of operands of logical operators is stopped once the overall result is known: in the case of the and operator, if the left argument evaluates to false, then the right argument is not evaluated and the whole expression evaluates to false.

requirements.subject: ent:and-operator
requirements.condition: the left operand evaluates to false
requirements.canonical: If the left operand of the `and` operator evaluates to `false`, the right operand IS NOT evaluated and the expression evaluates to `false`.
requirements.original: Short circuit evaluation for boolean expressions is used, i.e. the evaluation of operands of logical operators is stopped once the overall result is known: in the case of the and operator, if the left argument evaluates to false, then the right argument is not evaluated and the whole expression evaluates to false.

requirements.subject: ent:or-operator
requirements.condition: the left operand evaluates to true
requirements.canonical: If the left operand of the `or` operator evaluates to `true`, the right operand IS NOT evaluated and the expression evaluates to `true`.
requirements.original: In the case of the or operator, if the left argument evaluates to true, then the right argument is not evaluated and the whole expression evaluates to true.

requirements.subject: ent:bitwise-operator
requirements.canonical: The bitwise operators ARE bitwise not, bitwise and, bitwise or and bitwise xor.
requirements.original: The predefined bitwise operators perform the operations of bitwise not, bitwise and, bitwise or and bitwise xor.

requirements.subject: ent:bitwise-operator
requirements.canonical: The bitwise not, and, or and xor operators ARE named `not4b`, `and4b`, `or4b` and `xor4b` respectively.
requirements.original: These operators are known as not4b, and4b, or4b and xor4b respectively.

requirements.subject: ent:bitwise-operator
requirements.canonical: An operand of a bitwise operator SHALL be of root type bitstring, hexstring or octetstring.
requirements.original: Their operands shall be of root type `bitstring, hexstring or octetstring.

requirements.subject: ent:bitwise-operator
requirements.condition: the operator is and4b, or4b or xor4b
requirements.canonical: The two operands of the `and4b`, `or4b` and `xor4b` operators SHALL be of the same root type.
requirements.original: In the case of and4b, or4b and` xor4b the operands shall be of the same root types.The result type of the bitwise operators shall be the root type of the operands.

`ischosen` SHALL NOT be applied to a union/anytype template that is neither a specific value nor a value list (error).

requirements.subject: ent:ischosen-operator
requirements.condition: the operand is a value list
requirements.canonical: If the operand of `ischosen` is a value list, the operator returns `true` if all members of the value list have the referenced alternative selected.
requirements.original: In case of a value list, the operator returns true if all data objects present in the value list have the given alternative selected.

requirements.subject: ent:ischosen-operator
requirements.canonical: The `ischosen` operator returns `false` if there is another alternative of the union type or `anytype` for which `ischosen` would return `true`.
requirements.original: The result is false if there is another alternative of the union type or anytype on which ischosen would return true.

requirements.subject: ent:ischosen-operator
requirements.canonical: When determining the selected alternative of an `anytype`, type compatibility IS NOT considered; only the exact type chosen for the value satisfies `ischosen`.
requirements.original: NOTE: Note that in case of anytype-s, no type compatibility is considered when determining the selected alternative; i.e. at the evaluation only the exact type chosen for the given value will satisfy the above criteria.

requirements.subject: ent:isvalue-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isvalue` operator checks whether a referenced data object is a specific value.
requirements.original: The isvalue operator checks whether a referenced data object is a specific value.

requirements.subject: ent:isvalue-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isvalue` operator has the syntax `isvalue "(" TemplateInstance ")"`.
requirements.original: isvalue "(" TemplateInstance ")"

requirements.subject: ent:isvalue-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isvalue` operator returns `true` if its operand is completely initialized and resolves to a specific value.
requirements.original: The isvalue operator yields true, if the operand is completely initialized and resolves to a specific value.

requirements.subject: ent:optional-field
requirements.condition: the operand is of a record or set type
requirements.canonical: If the operand of `isvalue` is of a record or set type, an omitted optional field SHALL be considered as initialized.
requirements.original: If the operand is of record or set type, omitted optional fields shall be considered as initialized, i.e. the operator shall also yield true if optional fields of the operand are set to omit.

requirements.subject: ent:isvalue-operator
requirements.condition: the operand is of a record or set type
requirements.canonical: If the operand of `isvalue` is of a record or set type, the operator SHALL also return `true` when optional fields of the operand are set to `omit` (all other fields being specific values).
requirements.original: If the operand is of record or set type, omitted optional fields shall be considered as initialized, i.e. the operator shall also yield true if optional fields of the operand are set to omit.

requirements.subject: ent:isvalue-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isvalue` operator SHALL return `false` if its operand is not completely initialized or does not resolve to a specific value.
requirements.original: The operator shall yield false otherwise. The isvalue operator yields true, if the operand is completely initialized and resolves to a specific value.

requirements.subject: ent:null-value
requirements.canonical: For the `isvalue` operator, the special value `null` IS considered a specific value.
requirements.original: The specific value null is considered as concrete value.

ambiguity.issue: 'concrete value' is used instead of 'specific value' used in the rest of the clause.

requirements.subject: ent:isvalue-operator
requirements.canonical: `isvalue` applied to a union alternative IS different from `ischosen`: `isvalue` checks the content of the alternative, whereas `ischosen` checks whether the alternative has been selected.
requirements.original: // note, this is different from ischosen(mw_myUnion.ch1) as isvalue checks the content of the choice ch1, while ischosen is checking if ch1 has been selected or not

requirements.subject: ent:isbound-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isbound` operator checks whether a referenced data object is at least partially initialized.
requirements.original: The isbound operator checks whether a referenced data object is at least partially initialized.

requirements.subject: ent:isbound-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isbound` operator has the syntax `isbound "(" TemplateInstance ")"`.
requirements.original: isbound "(" TemplateInstance ")"

requirements.subject: ent:isbound-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isbound` operator returns `true` if its operand is at least partially initialized.
requirements.original: The isbound operator yields true, if the operand is at least partially initialized.

requirements.subject: ent:optional-field
requirements.condition: the operand is of a record or set type
requirements.canonical: If the operand of `isbound` is of a record or set type, an omitted optional field SHALL be considered as initialized.
requirements.original: If the operand is of a record or set type, omitted optional fields shall be considered as initialized, i.e. the operator shall also yield true if at least one optional field of the operand is set to omit.

requirements.subject: ent:isbound-operator
requirements.condition: the operand is of a record or set type
requirements.canonical: If the operand of `isbound` is of a record or set type, the operator SHALL return `true` if at least one optional field of the operand is set to `omit`.
requirements.original: set type, omitted optional fields shall be considered as initialized, i.e. the operator shall also yield true if at least one If the operand is of a record or optional field of the operand is set to omit.

requirements.subject: ent:isbound-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isbound` operator SHALL return `false` if its operand is not at least partially initialized.
requirements.original: The operator shall yield false otherwise. The isbound operator yields true, if the operand is at least partially initialized.

requirements.subject: ent:inaccessible-field
requirements.canonical: An inaccessible field (e.g. a non-selected alternative of a union, a subfield of an omitted record or set field, or a subfield of a non-selected union field) SHALL be considered as uninitialized.
requirements.original: Inaccessible fields (e.g. non-selected alternatives of union types, subfields of omitted record and set types or subfields of non-selected union fields) shall be considered as uninitialized, i.e. isbound shall yield for them false.

requirements.subject: ent:isbound-operator
requirements.canonical: The `isbound` operator SHALL return `false` for an inaccessible field.
requirements.original: Inaccessible fields (e.g. non-selected alternatives of union types, subfields of omitted record and set types or subfields of non-selected union fields) shall be considered as uninitialized, i.e. isbound shall yield for them false.

requirements.subject: ent:null-value
requirements.canonical: For the `isbound` operator, the special value `null` IS considered a specific value.
requirements.original: The specific value null is considered as concrete value.

ambiguity.issue: 'concrete value' is used instead of 'specific value'.

requirements.subject: ent:error
requirements.canonical: If the operand of `isbound` is not a reference (e.g. `v_myRec.f1/0`), a runtime error raised while evaluating the operand IS NOT suppressed by the presence checking error-handling rule.
requirements.original: checkResult := isbound(v_myRec.f1/0);   // shall cause an error already during evaluating the operand because the operand is not a reference and division by zero causes a runtime error

requirements.subject: ent:dot-notation
requirements.canonical: Within an expression, a field of a record or set type IS referenced with the dot notation `.field`.
requirements.original: Within expressions, fields of record and set types are referenced with the dot notation ".field".

requirements.subject: ent:index-notation
requirements.canonical: An element of a `record of`, `set of`, array or string type IS referenced with the index notation `[index]`.
requirements.original: Elements of record of, set of, array and string types are referenced with the index notation "[index]".

requirements.subject: ent:dot-notation
requirements.canonical: The dot `.` and the index brackets `[]` HAVE the same binding power.
requirements.original: Dot and brackets have the same binding power.

requirements.subject: ent:field-reference
requirements.canonical: Field references and list element references ARE evaluated from left to right.
requirements.original: Field references and list elements are evaluated from left to right.

requirements.subject: ent:decoded-field-reference
requirements.canonical: A decoded field reference IS a specific notation called decoding notation.
requirements.original: Decoded field reference is a specific notation called decoding notation that can be applied to expressions of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring or universal charstring types.

requirements.subject: ent:referenced-value
requirements.canonical: The decoding notation SHALL only be applied to expressions of type `bitstring`, `hexstring`, `octetstring`, `charstring` or `universal charstring`.
requirements.original: Decoded field reference is a specific notation called decoding notation that can be applied to expressions of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring or universal charstring types.

ambiguity.issue: 'can be applied to' may be a mere capability statement or an exclusive restriction. Chosen reading: exclusive restriction, as decoding requires a string-encoded payload.
readings: The decoding notation SHALL only be applied to expressions of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring or universal charstring types.
The decoding notation CAN be applied to expressions of these string types, without excluding other types.

requirements.subject: ent:decoded-field-reference
requirements.canonical: A decoded field reference IS used for accessing the content of implicitly decoded payload fields.
requirements.original: It is used for accessing content of implicitly decoded payload fields.

requirements.subject: ent:decoded-field-reference
requirements.canonical: A decoded field reference has the syntax `ReferencedValue "=>" ( PredefinedType | TypeIdentifier | ( "(" Type [ "," Expression ] ")" ) )`.
requirements.original:
ReferencedValue "=>" ( PredefinedType | TypeIdentifier | 
     ( "(" Type [ "," Expression ] ")" ) )

requirements.subject: ent:referenced-value
requirements.canonical: The ReferencedValue preceding the `=>` symbol in a decoding notation SHALL be decoded into a value of the type following the `=>` symbol.
requirements.original: The ReferencedValue preceding the => symbol in a decoding notation shall be decoded into a value of the type following the => symbol.

requirements.subject: ent:decoding-notation
requirements.canonical: A failure of decoding in a decoding notation SHALL cause a test case error.
requirements.original: Failure of this decoding shall cause a test case error. The ReferencedValue preceding the => symbol in a decoding notation shall be decoded into a value of the type following the => symbol.

requirements.subject: ent:encoding-format-parameter
requirements.condition: the ReferencedValue is of universal charstring type and the parenthesized syntax is used
requirements.canonical: If the ReferencedValue is of `universal charstring` type and the extended syntax with parentheses is used, the Type MAY be followed by an optional parameter defining the encoding format.
requirements.original: In case the ReferencedValue is of the universal charstring type and the extended syntax with parentheses is used, the Type can be followed by an optional parameter defining the encoding format.

requirements.subject: ent:encoding-format-parameter
requirements.canonical: The encoding format parameter of a decoding notation SHALL be of `charstring` type.
requirements.original: The parameter shall be of the charstring type and it shall contain one of the strings allowed for the decvalue_unichar function (specified in clause C.5.4).

requirements.subject: ent:encoding-format-parameter
requirements.canonical: The encoding format parameter of a decoding notation SHALL contain one of the strings allowed for the `decvalue_unichar` function (clause C.5.4).
requirements.original: The parameter shall be of the charstring type and it shall contain one of the strings allowed for the decvalue_unichar function (specified in clause C.5.4).

requirements.subject: ent:error
requirements.canonical: An encoding format parameter value other than the strings allowed for `decvalue_unichar` SHALL cause an error.
requirements.original: Any other value shall cause an error. The parameter shall be of the charstring type and it shall contain one of the strings allowed for the decvalue_unichar function (specified in clause C.5.4).

ambiguity.issue: The kind of error is not specified: a compile-time error when the value is known statically, or a runtime test case error.
readings: An invalid encoding format value SHALL cause a compile-time error if statically known, otherwise a test case error.
An invalid encoding format value SHALL always cause a runtime test case error.

requirements.subject: ent:encoding-format-parameter
requirements.condition: the ReferencedValue is not of universal charstring type
requirements.canonical: If the ReferencedValue is not of `universal charstring` type, the encoding format parameter SHALL NOT be present.
requirements.original: In case the ReferencedValue is not a universal `charstring, the optional parameter shall not be` present.

requirements.subject: ent:type-reference
requirements.condition: the type following => is not parenthesized
requirements.canonical: If the type following the `=>` symbol is not enclosed in parentheses, it SHALL be a built-in type or a type reference consisting of a single identifier.
requirements.original: a) If the type following the => symbol is not enclosed into parentheses, only a built-in type or a type reference consisting of a single identifier can be used.

requirements.subject: ent:type-reference
requirements.canonical: An extended type reference following the `=>` symbol SHALL always use the extended syntax with parentheses.
requirements.original: Extended type references shall always use the extended syntax with parentheses.

ambiguity.issue: 'Extended type reference' is not defined; it presumably means any type reference other than a built-in type or single identifier (e.g. qualified names or field sub-type references).

improper_terms.proper: type reference not consisting of a single identifier
